intro: You want a new book, a trip to the zoo and a pizza party. But you have only so much money and so much time. Every day, you have to choose. So does your family, your school and your town. This unit is about those choices.

First you will learn why we cannot have everything, and what we give up when we choose. Then you will visit a pizza shop and a paper airplane race. You will see how people make things, and why splitting up work helps.

By the end, you will be able to name the next-best thing you give up in a choice. You will sort resources into three groups. You will use a decision grid, and you will explain why people depend on each other.
bigQuestion: How do people make good choices when they cannot have everything they want?

timeline.t: People in Lydia, in what is now Turkey, make some of the first coins
Adam Smith writes The Wealth of Nations and describes splitting work in a pin factory
David Ricardo explains why countries gain when each makes what it does best
The Chicago Board of Trade opens, where people buy and sell grain
Henry Ford's company begins selling the Model T car
Ford's company starts a moving assembly line to build cars faster
Congress creates the Federal Reserve, with a bank in Chicago
The Great Depression begins, and many people lose their jobs
Families, schools and towns still face scarcity and make choices every day

words.d: when people want more than there is to go around, so they must choose
the next-best thing you give up when you make a choice
things from nature used to make goods, like soil, water and trees
the work and skills people use to make goods and services
tools, machines and buildings people make and use to make other goods and services
a reward or a cost that makes people more or less likely to do something
a person or business that makes goods or gives services
a person who buys and uses goods and services
doing one kind of job and getting very good at it
splitting a big job into smaller steps, with different people doing each step
when people rely on each other for goods and services
a person who starts a business and takes a risk to earn a profit

choices: Wanting more than there is to go around
test.why: Scarcity means wants are bigger than what there is.

test.q: Zoe picks swimming. Her next choice was the library. Her third was a nap. What is her opportunity cost?
test.why: Only the next-best choice, the library, is the opportunity cost.
A sewing machine is a tool people made to make other goods.

test.q: A class has $80. A trip costs $65 (example). How much is left?
A store gives a free drink with every 5 visits. What is the free drink?
test.why: It is a reward that makes people want to come back.
The barber gives a service, so the barber is a producer.

test.q: Team A makes 12 cards in 10 minutes. Team B splits the work and makes 18. How many more did Team B make?
Why does the division of labor often make more goods?
choices: Each worker gets fast at one step
It needs fewer resources of every kind
test.why: Repeating one step builds skill and saves switching time.

test.q: A lemonade stand spends $8 and sells 20 cups at $1 each (example). What is the profit?
What does a decision grid list down the side?
test.why: Choices go across the top. Criteria go down the side.

test.q: A storm stops trucks and stores run low on milk. What does this show?
test.why: Stores depend on trucks, and people depend on stores.

test.q: A line has steps that do 6, 3 and 5 parts a minute. About how many products a minute?
test.why: A line goes only as fast as its slowest step, 3 a minute.

test.q: Why do entrepreneurs take a risk?
choices: They spend money first and might not earn it back
test.why: They pay costs before they know how much they will sell.

test.q: A worker makes 4 bowls an hour, then 6 with a new wheel (example). How many more in 3 hours?
test.why: 3 times 4 is 12. 3 times 6 is 18. 18 minus 12 is 6.

write.prompt: Your class has $100 (an example amount) and three ideas: a game day for $60, new art supplies for $90, or a class plant garden for $40. Make a decision grid. Choose one idea. Name your opportunity cost, show the money left over, and explain why your choice is best.
tips: Put the choices across the top and what matters down the side.
Show the money: $100 minus the cost of your choice.
Name your opportunity cost: just the next-best idea.
Say one good thing you give up by not picking it.
